sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Abdominal Crunch Machine is a resistance-based exercise that targets the rectus abdominis through a controlled crunching motion.

The machine provides a fixed path of motion, making it easier to isolate the abs while supporting the lower back.

It is ideal for beginners learning to engage their core and for experienced lifters looking to add progressive overload to their ab training.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Isolates the abdominal muscles effectively
- Allows progressive overload with adjustable weight
- Supports the lower back throughout the movement
- Fixed path of motion ensures consistent form
- Suitable for all fitness levels
- Reduces strain on the neck compared to floor crunches
- Easy to track strength progress over time

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Rectus Abdominis

Secondary: Obliques, Hip Flexors, Serratus Anterior

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Adjust the seat height so your feet sit flat on the foot pads.
2. Sit with your back firmly against the back pad.
3. Grasp the handles or place your hands on the designated hand grips.
4. Position your chest against the chest pad if applicable.
5. Select an appropriate weight on the stack.
6. Sit upright with your core engaged and shoulders relaxed.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Exhale as you contract your abs and bring your torso forward towards your thighs.
2. Focus on curling your ribcage towards your pelvis rather than simply bending at the hips.
3. Squeeze your abs at the bottom of the movement for a brief pause.
4. Inhale as you slowly release the contraction and return to the starting position.
5. Maintain controlled movement throughout — avoid using momentum.
6. Repeat for the desired number of reps.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Using too much weight and relying on momentum
- Pulling with the arms instead of contracting the abs
- Bending at the hips rather than curling the spine
- Not controlling the eccentric (return) phase
- Holding breath throughout the movement
- Setting the seat too high or too low
- Rushing through reps without proper muscle engagement

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Abdominal Crunch Machine (plate-loaded or selectorized)
- Optional: Towel for comfort on the chest pad

sections.heading: Machine Adjustments
sections.content:
1. Adjust the seat so your feet rest flat on the foot pads.
2. The pivot point of the machine should align roughly with your mid-torso.
3. Adjust the chest pad or handles so you can comfortably reach them.
4. Select a weight that allows you to perform controlled reps.
5. Start light to learn the movement pattern before adding resistance.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Seat: Adjusted so feet are flat and knees are at roughly 90 degrees.
2. Back: Firmly pressed against the back pad.
3. Hands: Gripping the handles lightly — do not pull with your arms.
4. Core: Engaged before initiating the crunch.
5. Shoulders: Relaxed, not shrugged up towards the ears.
6. Head: Neutral position, avoid tucking the chin excessively.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Bodyweight Crunch: No equipment needed, targets the same muscles
- Cable Crunch: Kneeling crunch using a cable machine for resistance
- Decline Sit-Up: Increased range of motion on a decline bench
- Hanging Leg Raise: Advanced movement targeting lower abs
- Ab Rollout: Challenges the entire core through anti-extension
- Weighted Sit-Up: Free weight alternative for progressive overload

sections.heading: Crunch Variations
sections.content:
Machine Crunch: Standard selectorized or plate-loaded machine crunch
Cable Crunch: Kneeling crunch with cable resistance from above
Decline Crunch: Performed on a decline bench for greater range
Weighted Crunch: Floor crunch holding a plate or dumbbell
Reverse Crunch: Targets lower abs by lifting hips off the floor
Oblique Crunch: Rotational crunch to target the obliques

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Neck Pain: Machine crunch is a great option as it supports the neck
Lower Back Issues: Keep movement controlled and avoid excessive range of motion
No Machine Available: Use cable crunches or weighted floor crunches
Shoulder Injury: Adjust hand grip position or use a pad-style machine
Beginner: Start with bodyweight crunches to build baseline core strength
Hip Flexor Dominance: Focus on curling the ribcage down rather than bending at the hips
